newsitem.title: USA: U.S. doubts Cuba plane incident claims.
newsitem.headline: U.S. doubts Cuba plane incident claims.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday expressed scepticism about Cuban claims of incidents last week in which a U.S. Air Force plane came close to two civilian aircraft and advised Havana to "mind their own business."

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns made the comments after Cuba denounced what it said were incidents last week when a U.S. military plane supposedly flew north of the island and came excessively close to two civilian aircraft.
"First of all, we'll be happy to look into this. I can't believe it's true," Burns told reporters.

"Secondly, it is supremely ironic that the Cuban government would accuse the United States of unsafe air practices, considering the fact that they shot down two unarmed Cessnas on February 24th of 1996," he said.
Burns added, "They ought to mind their own business, and they ought to establish their own safety procedures before they cast stones at the United States."

A Cuban armed forces statement in ruling Communist Party newspaper Granma said the incidents on Friday involved a U.S. RC-135 plane that was carrying out "exploration against Cuba." The RC-135 is a four-engine tanker modified for reconnaissance.

In the first case, the Cuban statement said, a Panamanian DC-8 aircraft flying from Miami to Tocumen in Panama reported to Havana air traffic control on Friday morning that the U.S. Air Force plane had flown dangerously close to it at a point 70 miles (110 km) north of the central province of Ciego de Avila.

The Cuban statement said the U.S. plane flew at an altitude of 30,000 feet (9,000 metres) four miles (six km) from the Compania Panamena de Aviacion plane. It said the altitude difference was 1,500 feet (460 metres) rather than the 2,000 feet (610 metres) required.

Two hours later, the statement said, an American Airlines plane flying from Miami to Cancun, Mexico, reported to Havana air traffic control that it had spotted the same U.S. plane 60 miles (100 km) north of the western province of Pinar del Rio 15 miles (24 km) away. The altitude difference then was 1,000 feet (305 metres), the statement said.
It said Havana air traffic control reported both incidents to air traffic control in Miami. It said there had been 14 close flying incidents involving U.S. planes near Cuba this year.
